dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content: Hey there, kiddo. I’m Marnie Carter, ran this station for 32 years before I retired. Figured I’d drop by with spiced cocoa and welcome the crazy ornithologist willing to hike out here in late September for terns.

dialogue.speaker: Sam Riley
dialogue.content: Marnie! I would’ve recognized you from your tern migration papers even if you didn’t introduce yourself. Thanks for the cocoa, I haven’t had a hot drink since I got on the ferry this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content: Heard you’re here to finish that 5-year Arctic tern study you proposed back in 2019. Impressive. Most folks burn out after two field seasons out here, too busy chasing data to notice the place gets under their skin. Though I see you already found that old notebook of yours. Funny how the things we hide always find their way back to us, huh?

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Pull the unopened letter out of your pocket, admit you forgot you wrote it three years ago, and ask Marnie if she ever had to choose between her work and the person she loved.

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*The corner of her mouth tugs up, half sad, half amused, as she taps the carved seabird handle of her cane against the floorboard. She sets two mugs of cocoa down on the desk, one sliding across to you, steam curling up to fog the edge of your half-finished data spreadsheet. She taps the envelope with one gnarled, peppermint-scented finger, her silver braid slipping over her shoulder as she leans in.*
“Choose? Kiddo, that’s a lie folks tell themselves when they’re too scared to fight for both. I ran this station and raised two kids and was married to Clara for 42 years. Didn’t always get it right—missed our 10th anniversary because a tern colony got hit by a storm, she didn’t talk to me for three days. But I never chose one over the other. You wanna know the secret? That little red beacon out there? It’s not for the ships. It’s for the person you’re coming home to. Doesn’t dim the main lens one bit.”
*She nods at the envelope, then at the window where Old Red is just starting to glow pink against the tangerine sunset.* “You gonna open that, or you gonna spend the next 40 years wondering what it said?”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Tell Marnie you need to go down to the tidal pools first, to the time capsule you buried with Elara

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She barks a sharp, warm laugh, already pushing herself up from the desk with her cane, peppermints clinking in her coat pocket as she moves. She grabs a crumpled waterproof tarpaulin from the hook by the door and tosses it to you, her boot scuffing the edge of the whiteboard where that half-erased I love you still blots the corner.*
“Smart move. That note you two tucked in there? You’re gonna want that context before you read what Elara wrote you. And for the record—she’s the one who left that envelope on your desk three days ago. Came out on the early ferry, dropped it off, wouldn’t stick around ‘cause she said she didn’t wanna pressure you. Said she’d be waiting at the bench on the headland until sunset if you wanted to talk.”
*She jerks her chin toward the door, where the salt wind is already whistling through the cracks, carrying the faint cry of terns and the distant crash of swells against the rocks.* “C’mon. Tide’s going out in 20 minutes. You don’t wanna dig that box up when the waves are licking at your boots.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Head straight up to the headland bench to find Elara first, skip the time capsule entirely

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*Her eyebrows shoot up, but she gives a sharp, approving nod, already holding the office door open for you so the wind doesn’t yank it out of your hand. She shoves a crumpled peppermint into your palm as you pass, the smell of menthol cutting through the briny air blowing in off the water.* “Good. She’s been out there in that flimsy flannel for an hour, and that nor’easter rolling in’s gonna drop the temperature ten degrees before you even make it up the trail. For what it’s worth? She brought you a thermos of that ginger tea you used to chug by the gallon during 2021 nesting season. Still cares enough to remember the small stuff.”
*She nods toward the lighthouse, where Old Red has flickered to life, casting a faint red glow across the headland path. Over her shoulder, you spot the first dark, roiling storm clouds peeking over the western pine line, and the tern colony’s cries have turned sharp, skittish, warning of incoming weather.* “Hurry. Tide’s coming in fast, and that storm’ll knock the power out by sunset if it hits hard. You don’t wanna make her wait longer than she already has.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Pause to grab your waterproof field notebook first, to bring her the final tern data you finished compiling this morning

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content: *She snorts, but doesn’t stop you, leaning her cane against the doorframe as you dart back to the desk. The wind snatches the edge of your hoodie, and a sharp squawk from Tern 72 echoes through the open door, the little bird perched on the porch rail as if herding you along. She tosses you a second peppermint, her eyes crinkling at the corners when you fumble it before catching it.* “Wise choice. She’s been asking about your study every time she’s stopped by the general store this past year, never failed. Wants to hear every detail, even the boring stuff about nest success rates.” *She jabs her thumb at the window, where the first fat raindrop splatters against the glass, leaving a dark salt-stained splotch. The hum of the Fresnel lens picks up a faint, stuttering whine, the first warning of incoming power instability.* “Ten minutes, max, before that storm hits full force. If you’re not up that trail in two, I’m shoving you out the door myself, data notebook or no.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Tear out the final data summary page to bring, leave the full notebook locked in the desk to save time

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She barks a loud, cackling laugh, prodding the small of your back with her cane to herd you toward the door before you can second-guess yourself. Rain is now spattering against the porch in quick, cold bursts, and Old Red’s glow is already bleeding pink across the damp granite path, bright enough to cut through the growing dusk. Tern 72 squawks once, loud and sharp, before darting ahead of you down the trail, as if leading the way.*
“Finally using that brain of yours for something other than counting tern eggs, huh? Last thing you need right now is a bulky notebook weighing you down when you could be holding her hand instead. For the record? She didn’t wait all this time to read a 40-page dataset. She waited to see if you’d show up.”
*She shoves a crumpled plastic poncho into your free hand as you step over the threshold, the wind whipping your hair into your face. The lighthouse lens stutters again, dimming for half a second before flaring back to life.* “Go. I’ll hold down the station, and I’ll even dig that time capsule up for you tomorrow if the storm lets up. Just don’t keep her waiting.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Call Tern 72 to your shoulder for luck, letting the little bird perch there while you climb the trail, her tiny weight a familiar, warm reminder of all the good things you’re coming back to

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She leans against the doorframe, watching the bird flit down to settle light as a dandelion seed on your shoulder, her wings still fluttering slightly from the wind. Her expression softens, crinkles fanning around her eyes as she calls over the howl of the gale picking up around the lighthouse.* “Tern 72’s got better luck than any four-leaf clover out here. She sat on Clara’s shoulder the day I proposed, for Christ’s sake. You two are in good hands.”
*She points with her cane at the path ahead, where Old Red’s pink glow now paints the entire granite trail, so bright you can see every loose rock and gnarled pine root without a flashlight. The first rumble of thunder rolls in over the ocean, low and deep, and she taps the porch rail twice sharp, a silent reminder of the clock ticking down.*
*As you turn to start up the trail, she calls out one last time, loud enough to cut through the wind.* “Oh, and kiddo? That study’s already gonna get published. I sent your preliminary data to the journal last month when you weren’t looking. You don’t have anything left to prove to anyone but her.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Sprint up the trail as fast as your boots will carry you, the data page crinkling in your fist, ready to tell her you want both the work and her

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She whoops, loud enough to cut through the wind, waving her cane in the air as you take off up the path, Tern 72 clinging tight to your shoulder and squawking in time with your footfalls. Rain starts to sheet down in earnest now, plastering the hem of her oilskin coat to her calves, but she doesn’t move from the doorframe, watching until your figure vanishes around the bend in the trail, Old Red’s glow painting your back pink the whole way.*
*She turns back inside once you’re out of sight, already reaching for the receiver of the landline to call the ferry captain—she’d already made a deal with him earlier that day, holding off the last pre-storm departure for half an hour if it meant you two got the time you needed. She grins, popping a peppermint into her mouth as she leans against the desk, staring at that half-erased I love you scrawled on the whiteboard. The Fresnel lens stutters one last time before cutting out entirely, leaving only Old Red’s steady glow seeping through the windows.*
“Took you long enough, kiddo.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Cut to the ferry dock, where the captain is already gunning the engine, ready to pull away until he spots you two running toward the dock

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She’s leaning against the dock piling when you skid around the bend, Elara’s hand tangled in yours, rain plastering both your hair to your faces. She holds up a thermos of spiked cocoa in one hand, a crumpled ferry ticket in the other, and grins so wide the crinkles around her eyes disappear entirely. The ferry captain cuts the engine with a good-natured eye roll, leaning over the rail to wave you both aboard.*
“Told him I’d pay for his next month of blueberry pancakes if he waited five more minutes. Figured you two’d be cutting it close.” *She nods at the crumpled data page sticking out of your pocket, then at Elara’s grinning, rain-soaked face, and tosses you both a peppermint each. The rain lets up for half a second, just long enough for a sliver of sunset to paint the waves pink behind the lighthouse, Old Red’s glow still steady over the cove.* “See? Didn’t have to pick one. Just had to be brave enough to run fast enough to catch both.”

dialogue.speaker: System
dialogue.content: [MOMENTS LATER - EITHER ABOARD THE FERRY FOR THE MAINLAND, OR BACK TO THE RESEARCH STATION FOR THE STORM]

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Hand the data page to Elara right there on the dock, asking her to co-author the published study with you

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She leans her weight on her cane, watching Elara’s face go from shocked, to wobbly, to grinning so wide she snorts, half rain and half happy tears dripping down her cheeks as she throws her arms around you. The ferry horn blares once, sharp and impatient, and Marnie snorts, jabbing the dock with her cane to get your attention, already backing toward the trail that leads back to the station. A faint silver glint of a journal acceptance email peeks out from the pocket of her oilskin coat, the one she’d been hiding for three weeks, waiting for the right moment.* “Hold that thought, you two. The journal sent the official acceptance this morning. I brought the hard copy with me—figured you’d want to sign off on the co-author line together after you two get back from the mainland.”
*The wind picks up again, whipping Tern 72 off the rail where she’d been perched, the little bird circling over your heads once before darting back toward the lighthouse. The captain yells that they’re leaving in 60 seconds, and Marnie waves you both toward the gangplank, already turning to trudge up the trail, Old Red’s glow painting the back of her coat pink.* “And for the record? Clara and I are throwing you two a celebration dinner when you get back. No talk of terns allowed. Well… maybe a little. Don’t be late.”

dialogue.speaker: System

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Turn back to the station with Elara, choosing to wait out the storm together at the place you built your first home

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She pauses halfway up the trail, cane planted firm in the mud, and huffs a laugh loud enough to carry over the wind, not even pretending to be surprised. She waves a hand like she knew you’d choose this all along, already turning back toward the dock to yell at the captain, who just grunts and nods, pulling the gangplank up and gunning the engine to head back to the mainland early. The rain softens to a fine mist when you two catch up to her, Tern 72 darting out from under the porch overhang to land on Elara’s shoulder now, pecking playfully at the brim of her red cap.*
“Figured you’d pick the lighthouse. I already stoked the fireplace, made a pot of that spiced cocoa you both like, and dug up the time capsule an hour ago. It’s sitting on the kitchen table next to the acceptance hard copy.” *She prods your calf gently with the tip of her cane as the three of you trudge up the path, Old Red’s glow wrapping around you like a blanket, warm and steady even as the storm rumbles louder out over the Atlantic.* “Clara’s gonna bring the blueberry pancakes tomorrow once the storm passes. You two have got all the time in the world now.”

dialogue.speaker: User
dialogue.content: Head straight to the kitchen to crack open the time capsule and sign the co-author line together tonight

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*She holds the station door open for you both, the warm, cinnamon-spiced air spilling out to wrap around your rain-chilled cheeks, and taps the edge of the kitchen table with her cane once you’re inside. The time capsule box sits there, dented metal glinting in the firelight, the acceptance letter fanned open next to it, a blank line for the second co-author waiting neat at the top of the page. She tosses you both wool socks from the pile by the door, then snags her sketchbook off the counter, already heading for the stairs up to her quarters.*
“Figured you’d want the space to yourselves. I’ll be up in the lantern room making sure Old Red stays lit through the storm—yell if you need more marshmallows for the cocoa. And for the record? That note you two wrote in the capsule three years ago? I peeked. You were always gonna keep that promise.” *She winks, pulling the door to the stairs shut behind her, leaving the two of you alone with the crackle of the fire and the distant roar of the waves. Tern 72 flutters down to perch on the fridge handle, eyeing the jar of peanut butter on the counter like she’s plotting a heist.*

*Halfway up the stairs, I hear the scratch of pen on paper and pause, pressing my back to the wall to listen to you two laugh, Elara teasing you for your messy signature like you did three years ago when you carved your initials into the bench. A soft clink of the cocoa mugs hitting the table follows, then the scrape of the time capsule lid being pried open. I pull the journal acceptance draft I’ve kept folded in my sweater pocket for three weeks out, tucking it into my sketchbook next to the charcoal drawing I did of you two last summer, huddled over the tern nest with Tern 72 perched on your shoulder. The Fresnel motor hums under my boots, and I smile to myself, rapping twice on the stairwell door so you know I’m nearby.*
The pen’s blue, same as the one you used to scrawl that terrible I love you on the office whiteboard! *I call down the stairs, already heading up to the lantern room, the wind whistling through the upper vents as Old Red’s glow spills through the crack in the door. A sharp squawk from Tern 72 echoes up the stairs, followed by a yelp from Elara—looks like the peanut butter heist is already in progress.* And if that thieving bird steals half your sandwich, don’t say I didn’t warn you!

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter

*I hear the commotion below—shouts of glee, the scrape of a kitchen chair skidding across the floor, Tern 72’s indignant squawks as she flutters from the counter to the top of the bookshelf, peanut butter smudged on her beak. I snort, leaning over the stair railing to peer down at the chaos, and fish a crumpled sunflower seed bag out of my oilskin pocket, tossing it down so it lands at your feet. The seed bag bursts open when it hits the floor, spilling golden kernels across the rug.*
“Quit terrorizing the bird, kiddo—she’s just got better priorities than paperwork right now.” *I tap the lantern room door behind me, where Old Red’s steady red glow bleeds out around the frame, soft and warm. I hold up the charcoal drawing I tucked in my sketchbook, waving it once so you can catch a glimpse of the two of you hunched over the tern nest from last summer.* “Once you wrangle her, bring that acceptance letter and the note from the capsule up here. I’ve got a surprise for you both—Clara dropped off the printed page proofs this morning, and the lighthouse gallery’s got the best light for photos. You two are gonna want to remember this.”

dialogue.speaker: Marnie Carter
dialogue.content:
*I cackle as Tern 72 dive-bombs the sunflower seeds first, leaving half the peanut butter jar teetering on the bookshelf edge, and yank the lantern room door wide open so the warm red glow of Old Red spills down the stairwell to meet you. The Fresnel lens hums loud enough to vibrate the soles of your boots when you step inside, the 1950s motor thrumming under the sound of the storm. I set out three chipped mugs of cocoa on the gallery railing, steam curling up to fog the cold glass, and slide the printed page proofs across the rail toward you—your name and Elara’s, both printed bold at the top, next to a full-page photo of Tern 72 perched on the headland bench. I tap the edge of the time capsule with my cane, nodding at the metal box tucked under your arm.*
“Clara also left a second note with the proofs. She already reserved you two a two-year station extension, funding fully approved, starts next month. No more choosing between the terns and each other. You two earned it.” *I lean against the railing, sipping my cocoa, and nod down at the cove where the waves are starting to calm, the first hints of starlight peeking through the storm clouds overhead.* “Now open that box. I’ve been waiting three years to see you two read that note out loud.”

*I lean back against the railing, cocoa mug warming my calloused palms, as you two fumble with the old cast-iron switch for Old Red—the same one the keeper who installed it used, chipped paint flaking off the toggle under your fingers. The red glow blooms slow first, soft, then bleeds out across the cove, painting Elara’s freckles pink, gilding the edges of the acceptance letter you’re still clutching, even turning the salt crust on the windowsill look like crushed rose petals. I nod at the time capsule box tucked in the crook of your arm, then tap the stack of extra stationery I set on the windowsill next to the cocoa mugs, embossed with the Cape Halcyon Research Station logo.*
“Rituals stick, kiddo. That’s the point.” *I nod at the note peeking out from the time capsule, then at the blank paper. “Once you read that old promise out loud, you get to write a new one. To leave for the version of you two that digs this box up three years from now. No more trade-offs. No more ‘either/or.’ Write whatever you want.”*

*I lean forward, elbows propped on the cold gallery railing, and watch the purple of the old pressed sprig catch the red glow of Old Red, soft next to the bright, dewy fresh one you tuck beside it. The scent of salt and lavender hits the air, sharp and sweet, and for a second I’m right back there 40 years ago, burying a box just like this with my wife under that same heart-shaped rock. I pull my leather-bound journal out from under my arm, flipping to a crumpled, yellowed note tucked between the pages—our old promise, scrawled in the same blue marker you use for your data tallies—and tap it once against the time capsule lid.*
“My wife and I wrote ours on a stormy night just like this. Said we’d run the station together for five years, and we ended up staying 30. Rituals aren’t about getting the future right, they’re about telling the person next to you you’re gonna show up for it, whatever it looks like.” *I nod at the blank sheet of stationery, then slide a fountain pen I’ve had since I was 19 across the sill to you, the nib worn smooth from decades of use.* “Go on. Let’s hear what the two of you have got planned for the next three years.”
